dek: Ted Sevransky, who sells picks as Teddy Covers, is a Las Vegas bettor and betting media regular. He sells through StatSalt and WagerTalk, two sites run by the same company, with picks from $25 and passes up to $1,999 a year. Sales are final, the optional guarantee pays in store credit, and every record on his pages is chosen or graded by the seller.

short_answer: Teddy Covers is a real, well known name. Ted Sevransky has sold picks and appeared on betting shows for years, and his picks are sold by Wager Talk Media, LP, a company that names itself as the seller and gives a Las Vegas address. In that sense he is legitimate: you pay, and you get picks with written analysis.

Whether his picks make money for a buyer is a separate question, and nothing we could open answers it. His pages show hot streaks such as "8-4 (67%)" over three weeks and "2-1 (67%) YTD", graded by the company that sells the picks. The one list with lines and prices, his WagerTalk Last 20, was 10-10 on 7 Nov 2026. Forum posts from 2010 and 2013 claimed long losing football runs, but those are old and unverified.

Treat Teddy Covers as an experienced seller with marketing records, not a proven winner. If you buy, buy short, record every pick with the line you actually got, and judge it after a few hundred picks.

guarantee: StatSalt's refund policy says purchases are made from Wager Talk Media, LP and that "All Sales are Final and products are sold 'as is'." It says no refund is issued once a product is purchased, delivered or viewed, including when a buyer cannot legally bet a game in their state or an email or text never arrives. The StatSalt terms add that the buyer's exclusive remedy is a refund or replacement "at our option", so the choice belongs to the seller.

On WagerTalk some of his daily picks carry a guarantee option that costs more: the college football 4 pack was $29 plain or $44 guaranteed, and the NFL pick $25 or $38. The guarantee box says that if the daily package does not show "an overall profit across all included plays," the paid cash value is "credited back to your account to be used on a future purchase." That is store credit for paying about 50% more, not cash, and it never covers losses on the bets themselves.
The StatSalt FAQ says subscriptions can be cancelled at any time from account settings, with access running to the end of the billing period. We did not see whether his passes renew automatically.

claims_note: Most of these numbers are short windows or slices chosen by the seller: three weeks, ten days, plays rated 4% or higher, 5% plays only. A college football "2-1 (67%)" is three games. The largest figure, 545-457 in the NBA since 2022, works out to about 54% winners, a modest edge if real, but we could not open the log behind it, and it does not say what price each play was graded at.
Featured packages and streaks on these pages change from day to day, and on 7 Nov 2026 the same 3 day pass was priced differently on the two sites. Check the page on the day you buy.
record: What is independently verifiable: nothing we found today. We found no full, time stamped log of every Teddy Covers pick kept by a third party, no published contest results, and no court or regulator records about him in our searches.

What is the seller's own record: WagerTalk shows a Last 20 list with date, side, line, price and result. On 7 Nov 2026 it ran from 31 Oct to 6 Nov 2026 and showed 10 wins and 10 losses, mostly at prices between -106 and -119. StatSalt shows a shorter Latest Picks list with game and result but no line or price. Both lists, and every streak above, are graded by Wager Talk Media, the company that sells his picks.

Old forum posts point the other way but carry little weight: in 2013 a Sportsbook Review member posted totals he said he tracked for the 2012 to 2013 season showing large losses, and in 2010 Las Vegas Advisor members posted losing football records. Neither cited a source we could check.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition Teddy Covers is not matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how his picks perform.

customers_intro: Independent customer evidence on Teddy Covers is thin and mostly old. We found no recent buyer reviews of him by name. Below is everything we found and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: A Sportsbook Review member said he tracked Teddy Covers from the start of the 2012 college football season to see what a loyal subscriber would make. He posted season totals of 33-41-1 in college football (down 112 units), 40-42-1 in the NFL (down 65 units), 43-53 in the NBA and 48-42-5 in college basketball, and said football alone lost 177 units. He posted part of a pick list but no source, and we did not verify the figures.

On the Las Vegas Advisor forum, a member called him "as good a pro capper as there is" and praised his baseball picks, while noting a hard football season. Another member in the same thread said he liked Teddy and thought he was bright.

In the same thread, a member posted football records of 109-113-1 for 2009 and 55-78-4 for 2010 to that date, and another recalled an ad for a "67% CBB Big Ticket Run" that he said was only 2-1 over the last three plays. A third member answered that the football sample was not large. None of these figures came with a log we could check.

We found no Reddit thread about Teddy Covers, CapperTek showed no reviews of him, and Trustpilot pages for StatSalt and WagerTalk did not load for our check. We found no recent customer reviews of him by name.

conflicts: Wager Talk Media, LP sells his picks on both StatSalt and WagerTalk and also grades the records shown beside them. The scorekeeper and the store are the same company, which earns money on every sale.

The StatSalt footer says that if a reader clicks a link to a bookmaker or casino and opens an account, "StatSalt may receive a commission." We did not see the terms of any deal, but the site has an interest in readers opening betting accounts.
strengths: A named seller, Wager Talk Media, LP, with a Las Vegas address and written refund, guarantee and cancellation terms.
WagerTalk shows his last 20 picks with the line and price, losses included, which is more than many sellers show.
Free picks with full written analysis are posted on both profiles, so you can judge his reasoning before paying.
concerns: No full public record. Every streak is a short window or slice chosen and graded by the seller.
All sales are final. The guarantee costs about 50% more and returns store credit, never cash, and never covers betting losses.
His own domain, teddycovers.com, showed a parking page, so buyers depend on the reseller's pages.
checklist: Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Count units, not wins. A 60% record at heavy favorites can still lose money.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Most "guarantees" in this business are credits.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: Yes in the sense that Ted Sevransky is a real, long time Las Vegas bettor whose picks are sold by a named company with an address and written terms. We could not verify that his picks win over time, because no full record of every pick is published.
How much does Teddy Covers cost?

On 7 Nov 2026 single picks and packages ran $25 to $49, all sports passes were $39 for a day and $99 for 7 days, and WagerTalk listed $299 for 30 days, $749 for 90 days and $1,999 for a year. A guaranteed version of some daily picks cost more, such as $44 instead of $29.
Does Teddy Covers have a verified record?
No. The streaks on his pages and his WagerTalk Last 20 (10-10 on 7 Nov 2026) are graded by the company that sells his picks, and we found no third party log. Watchdog has no graded record for him.

For the money you get picks with written analysis from an experienced bettor, from $25 a pick. What is unproven is whether a buyer beats the roughly 52.4% needed at -110 over hundreds of picks, and sales are final, with only an optional store credit guarantee.
